clinicalPearls: A paradoxical sensation of nasal obstruction and difficulty breathing despite an objectively wide, patent nasal airway
It is typically iatrogenic, following extensive turbinate reduction or resection
Patients describe a feeling of suffocation, nasal dryness, crusting and a distressing loss of awareness of airflow
There is often a significant burden of anxiety, low mood and sleep disturbance
Diagnosis is clinical, correlating symptoms with a history of turbinate surgery and a paradoxically open nasal cavity
Management is challenging and includes humidification, nasal conditioning and, in selected cases, procedures to augment tissue
reference.pathophysiology: Empty nose syndrome is attributed to loss of functional turbinate tissue, which normally regulates nasal airflow, resistance, humidification and sensation. Excessive turbinate reduction disrupts laminar airflow and the mucosal sensory feedback (including cooling detected by nasal receptors) that generates the perception of comfortable breathing, so patients feel obstructed despite a wide airway. Impaired air conditioning also causes dryness, crusting and mucosal dysfunction, and the distressing symptoms are compounded by neurosensory and psychological factors.
additionalInvestigations: History correlating symptoms with prior turbinate surgery
Nasal endoscopy documenting the wide cavity and mucosal state
Cotton test placing tissue where turbinate was removed to gauge symptom relief
Assessment of mood, anxiety and sleep
Exclusion of coexisting rhinosinusitis or atrophic rhinitis
redFlags: Severe psychological distress or suicidal ideation
Features suggesting atrophic rhinitis with secondary infection
reference.prognosis: The condition is often chronic and difficult to treat; conservative measures and, in some, augmentation procedures can improve symptoms, but outcomes are variable and psychological support is frequently needed.
pitfalls: Dismissing the complaint because the airway looks widely patent
Performing further tissue-removing surgery that worsens symptoms
Confusing it with ordinary structural obstruction or rhinosinusitis
management: First-line conservative care with nasal humidification, saline irrigation, sprays and emollient ointment to relieve dryness, crusting and the paradoxical sensation of obstruction
Nasal conditioning measures to improve air humidification and mucosal health
Surgical augmentation of the nasal cavity with implants or grafts to restore lost turbinate bulk and airflow resistance in selected refractory cases
Use of the cotton test to predict likely benefit from tissue augmentation before surgery
Assessment and treatment of the associated anxiety, low mood and sleep disturbance, with psychological support
Exclusion and treatment of coexisting rhinosinusitis or atrophic rhinitis
Otolaryngology referral to a specialist familiar with the condition given its challenging, often chronic course
